sections.section_title: Nityārcanā: The Sequences of Daily Worship
sections.content:
The chapter begins by defining Nityārcanā as daily worship, an elaborate procedure with either sixteen (Ṣoḍaśopacāra) or five (Pañcopacāra) major sequences. The sixteen sequences, according to the Bṛhat-parāśara-saṃhitā, are detailed in a specific order: (1) āvāhanā (invocation), (2) āsana (providing seat), (3) pādya (offer of water for the feet), (4) arghya (respectful libation), (5) ācamana (water for ceremonial sipping), (6) snāna (providing a bath), (7) vastra (drying up the deity and offering clean garments), (8) upavīta (providing a sacred cord), (9) gandha (offering sandal-paste), (10) puṣpa (decorating with flowers), (11) dhūpa (burning incense), (12) dīpa (waving of lights), (13) naivedya (offering of food), (14) namaskāra (prostrations), (15) pradakṣiṇa (circumambulation), and (16) udvāsana (send-off). An accompanying Sanskrit verse from the Bṛhat-parāśara-saṃhitā outlines this process: 

यथावाहयेद्दवमृचा च पुरुषोत्तमम् ।
द्वितीययासनं दद्यात्पाद्यं तृतीयया ।।
अर्घ्यं चतुर्थ्या दात्व्यं पञ्चम्यायमनं तथा।
षष्ट्या स्नानं प्रकुर्वीत सप्तम्या वस्त्रधौतकम् ॥
यज्ञोपवीतं चाष्टम्या नवम्या गन्धमेव च।
पुष्पं देयं दशम्या त्वैकादश्या च धूपकम् ।।
द्वादश्या दीपकं दद्यात् त्रयोदश्या निवेदयेत्।
चतुर्दश्या नमस्कारं पञ्चदश्या प्रदक्षिणाः।
षोडश्योद्वासनं कुर्यात् ...॥

An alternative sixteen-step sequence is also presented: (1) pādya, (2) arghya, (3) ācamanīya, (4) snāna, (5) vasana (vastra), (6) bhūśaṇa (decorating with jewels), (7) gandha, (8) puṣpa, (9) dhūpa, (10) dīpa, (11) naivedya, (12) ācamana, (13) tāmbūla (betel-nut and leaves), (14) arcanā-stotra (eulogy), (15) tarpaṇa (fire-oblations), and (16) namaskāra.

पाद्यार्घ्यचमनीयं च स्नानं वसन वसनभूषणे ।
गन्धपुष्पधूपदीनैवेद्यामनं तथा ॥
ताम्बूलमर्चनस्तोत्रं तर्पणं च नमास्क्रियां।
प्रयोजयेत्प्रपूजायां उपचारास्तुं षोडश ॥

When shortened to five sequences, it is called pañcopacāra-pujā, consisting of (1) gandha, (2) puṣpa, (3) dhūpa, (4) dīpa, and (5) naivedya.

गन्धः सुमं तथा धूपदीपौ नैवेद्यमेव च ।
पञ्चोपचारा एते स्युर्दीपान्तं वापि सम्मतम्॥

An even shorter three-sequence worship involves (1) snāna, (2) pūjā, and (3) naivedya, where 'pūjā' can encompass details like puṣpa, gandha, dhūpa, and dīpa.

स्नानं पूजा च नैवेद्यमुपचारास्त्रयः क्रमात्।
sections.summary: This section introduces Nityārcanā, or daily worship, and outlines its primary forms. It details the classical sixteen-step worship (Ṣoḍaśopacāra) as per the Bṛhat-parāśara-saṃhitā, provides an alternative sixteen-step sequence, and describes the shorter five-step (Pañcopacāra) and three-step worship procedures.

sections.content:
Texts like Śaiva-ratnākara describe the specific spiritual and material benefits (phala) obtained from each sequence of worship. 
- **āvāhana** (invocation): yields the benefit of a fire ritual ('kratu-phalam').
- **āsana** (seat): grants the status of Indra ('śukra-tattvam').
- **pādya** (water for feet): destroys sins ('pātakam hanyāt').
- **arghya** (water of honour): makes one worthy of honour ('āpnoty arghyatām').
- **ācamana** (sipping): brings peace of mind and happiness ('sucittaḥ sukhitam').
- **snāna** (bathing): eliminates fear of disease ('vyādhi-bhayam hanyāt').
- **vastra** (garments): increases lifespan ('āyuṣya-vardhanam').
- **upavīta** (sacred cord): makes one eligible for the gnosis of Brahman ('brahma-vetṛtvam').
- **bhūṣaṇa** (decorations): secures one's welfare ('anapadyam avāpnuyāt').
- **gandha** (sandal-paste): fulfills all desires ('labhate kāmam').
- **akṣata** (consecrated rice): ensures non-destruction ('akṣatām bhavet').
- **puṣpa** (flowers): secures the kingdom of paradise ('svarga-rājyam avāpnuyāt').
- **dhūpa** (incense): burns away sins ('dahati pāpāni').
- **dīpa** (lights): prevents untimely death ('mṛtyu-vināśanaḥ').
- **naivedya** (food): brings contentment ('tṛptirato bahavet').
- **mukha-vāsa** (betel-leaves): makes the devotee celebrated ('kīrtimān bhavati dhruvam').
- **nīrājana** (waving light): purifies the heart ('śuddhātmā').
- **pradakṣiṇa** (circumambulation): destroys sins ('pāpam hanti').
- **praṇāma** (prostrations): ensures innumerable years in heaven ('vasate svarge dehānte').
- **stotra** (eulogies): makes one immediately eloquent ('vāgmī bhavati tat-kṣaṇāt').
sections.summary: This section, referencing the Śaiva-ratnākara, enumerates the specific benefits—spiritual, physical, and metaphysical—associated with performing each of the individual steps in the sequence of worship, from gaining merits of a fire ritual to destroying sins and attaining eloquence.

sections.section_title: Preparatory Rites for the Priest: Sandhyā
sections.content:
Regardless of the number of sequences, daily temple worship requires the priest to undergo preliminary purification rites. A twice-born priest must perform his customary sandhyā (twilight prayers) before coming to the temple.

उपवीती बद्धशिखः स्वाचान्तो द्विरनाकुलः ।
प्राङ्मुख सततं विप्रः सन्ध्योपासनमाचरेत्।।
सन्ध्या येन न विज्ञाता सन्ध्या येनानुपासिता ।
जीवमानो भवेच्छूद्रः मृतः श्वा चैव जायते ॥

The chapter highlights that in Śaivāgama texts, two types of sandhyās are prescribed. The first is the ordinary `vaidika-sandhyā`, which is required for every twice-born person. The second is the `Śaiva-sandhyā`, which is obligatory for a priest initiated into Śaivāgama. The Vaidika sandhyā must be performed first, followed by the Śaiva-sandhyā.

वैदिकीं तु पुरा कृत्वा पश्चाच्छैवमथाचरेत्।
दीक्षा संस्कारहीनस्य शुद्धवैदिकमुच्यते ॥

A similar distinction exists in the Śākta-tāntrik tradition, where the second sandhyā is known as `tāntriki-sandhyā`.
sections.summary: This section details the necessary preparatory rituals for a temple priest. It emphasizes the mandatory performance of sandhyā (twilight prayers) and distinguishes between the universal Vaidika sandhyā and the specialized, initiatory Śaiva-sandhyā (or Tāntriki-sandhyā in Śākta traditions), which must be performed in sequence.

sections.content:
The purpose of the `tāntriki-sandhyā` is to gain eligibility for the worship of a particular deity. A key part of this is the ceremonial sipping of water (ācamana) thrice, mentioning the three principles (tattvas): ātmā (self), vidyā (knowledge), and śiva (auspiciousness).

आत्मतत्त्वाय स्वाहा।
विद्यातत्त्वाय स्वाहा।
शिवतत्त्वाय स्वाहा।

This is followed by other rites like aṅga-nyāsa, kara-nyāsa, etc. The Gāyatrī mantra for this sandhyā is given:

ॐ तत्पुरुषाय विद्महे।
महादेवाय धीमहि।
तन्नो रुद्रः प्रचोदयात्।।

The chapter then introduces the concept of `Nyāsa`, which means placement, assignment, or mental appropriation. It is a ritual involving the placement of deities, seed-letters (bīja-mantras), or mantras on various parts of one's own body or the deity's body. The purpose is to eliminate obstacles and ensure the success of the main ritual (like mantra-japa or worship). The definition is given as:

पुजाजपादेः प्रग्विघ्ननाशमन्त्रसिध्यर्थं देहान्तर्बहिश्च
वर्णादि विन्यासः।

Nyāsa can be performed as a daily routine or during specific religious acts.
sections.summary: This section explains the specialized tāntriki-sandhyā and introduces the pivotal concept of Nyāsa. Nyāsa is defined as a ritual of 'placement' of divine energies or mantras onto the body to purify the practitioner, remove obstacles, and ensure the success of the worship.

sections.content:
The text explains that Nyāsa is performed at various times, as stated in the Yoginī-hṛdaya:

प्रातः काले च वा पूजासमये होमकर्मणि ।
जपकालेऽपि वा तेषां विनियोगः पृथक् पृथक् ॥

The usual nyāsa is `ṣaḍ-aṅga-nyāsa` (six-limbed nyāsa), which involves six parts of the body (`aṅga-nyāsa`) and the five fingers plus palm/back (`kara-nyāsa`). An example of `mātṛkā-nyāsa` is provided, beginning with kara-nyāsa (placement on the hands):

1. अंक खं गं घं ङ आं अङ्‌‌गुष्ठाभ्यां नमः। (Thumb)
2. इं चं छं जं झं जं ई तर्जनीभ्यां नमः। (Forefinger)
3. उं टं ठं ढं णं ऊं मध्यामाभ्यां नमः। (Middle finger)
4. एं तं थं दं धं नं ऐं अनामिकाभ्यां नमः (Ring finger)
5. ओं पंफ बीं भं औं कनिष्ठिकाभ्यां नमः। (Little-finger)
6. यं रं लं वंशं षं सं हं लं अ करतलकरपृष्ठाय नमः। (Palm and its back)

Aṅga-nyāsa must follow kara-nyāsa. The six 'limbs' of the nyāsa mantra itself are `ṛṣi` (sage), `chandas` (metre), `devatā` (deity), `bīja` (seed), `śakti` (energy), and `kīlaka` (pillar), which are placed on the head, mouth, heart, private part, feet, and entire body, respectively. 

ऋषिं न्यसेन्मूर्ध्नि छन्दस्तु मुखपङ्कजे ।
देवतां हृदयं चैव बीजं तु गुह्यदेशके ।
शक्तिं च पादयोश्चैव सर्वांगे कीलकं न्यसेत्॥

The aṅga-nyāsa takes this form:
1. अंकं खं गं घं डं आं हृदयाय नमः।
2. इं चं छं जं झं जं ई शिरसे स्वाहा।
3. उं टं ठं डं ढं णं ऊं शिखायै वषट्।
4. एं तं थं दं नं ऐं कवचाय हूं।
5. ओं पंफ बीं भं में औं नेत्रत्रयाय वौषट्।
6. यं रं लं वंशं षं सं हं लं अस्त्राय फट् ॥

The meanings of the concluding mantra words (`namaḥ`, `svāhā`, etc.) are given as offering/dedication, with `phaṭ` signifying the elimination of obstacles. The text states that through nyāsa, the devotee attains a divine status, quoting, `'nādevo devam arcayet'` (one who is not a deity himself should not worship the deity).
sections.summary: This section provides a detailed breakdown of Nyāsa, focusing on the common six-limbed (ṣaḍ-aṅga) form, which comprises kara-nyāsa (on the hands) and aṅga-nyāsa (on the body). It explains the components of a mantra for nyāsa (ṛṣi, chandas, etc.) and demonstrates how performing nyāsa transforms the worshipper into a divine being, fit to perform worship.

sections.content:
The number and type of ritual placements differ according to sectarian traditions. 

**Vaiṣṇava-sects (worship of Viṣṇu):** Six placements are involved.
1. Keśava-kīrtyādi-nyāsa
2. mūrti-pañjara-nyāsa
3. tattva-nyāsa
4. bhūti-pañjara-nyāsa
5. daśāṅga-nyāsa
6. pañcāṅga-nyāsa

**Śaiva sects (worship of Śiva):** Seven placements are involved.
1. śrīkaṇṭhādi-nyāsa
2. īśānādi-pañca-mūrti-nyāsa
3. mantra-nyāsa
4. mūrti-nyāsa
5. golaka-nyāsa
6. subhagādi-nyāsa
7. bhūṣaṇa-nyās

**Śrī-vidyā cult:** Twenty-two placements are prescribed.
1. vaśinyādi-nyāsa
2. nava-yonyātmaka-nyāsa
3. pīṭha-nyāsa
4. tattva-nyāsa
5. pañcadaśī nyāsa
6. ṣoḍaśi-nyāsa
7. saṃhāra-nyāsa
8. sthiti-nyāsa (listed twice)
9. sṛṣṭi-nyāsa
10. nāda-nyāsa
11. ṣoḍhā-nyāsa
12. gaṇeśa-nyāsa
13. graha-nyāsa
14. nakṣatra-nyāsa
15. yoginī-nyāsa
16. rāśi-nyāsa
17. tripurā-nyāsa
18. ṣoḍaśā-nityā-nyāsa
19. kāma-rati-nyāsa
20. sṛṣṭi-mati-nyāsa
21. prakaṭa-yoginī-nyāsa
22. āyudha-nyāsa
sections.summary: This section illustrates the diversity of ritual practice by outlining the different sets of Nyāsa performed in major Hindu traditions. It lists the six types used in Vaiṣṇava sects, the seven in Śaiva sects, and the extensive list of twenty-two nyāsas prescribed in the Śrī-vidyā cult.

sections.content:
The chapter broadly classifies nyāsas into two varieties: `Rṣyādi-nyāsa` and `Ṣaḍaṅga-nyāsa`. An example of `svaprāṇa-pratiṣṭhā` (placement of the deity in one's own body) is given to illustrate Rṣyādi-nyāsa, where the core components are placed on the body:
1. Seers (Brahma, Viṣṇu, Maheśvara) on the head: ॐ ब्रह्मविष्णुमहेश्वरऋषिभ्यो नमः शिरसि ॥
2. Metres (Ṛg, Yajus, Sāma) on the mouth: ॐ ऋग्यजुः सामछन्देभ्यो नमः मुखे ॥
3. Deity (Prāṇaśakti) in the heart: ॐ प्राणशक्त्यै नमः हृदये।
4. Seed-syllable (bīja) in the genital region: ॐ बीजाय मनः गुह्ये॥
5. Power (śakti, as hrīṃ) on the feet: ॐ ह्रीं शक्तये नमः पादयोः ॥
6. Peg (kīlaka, as Krauṃ) all over the body: ॐ क्रौं कीलकाय नमः सर्वांगे ॥

Following this, a more complex `ṣaḍaṅga-nyāsa` is described. This version involves not just letters of the alphabet, but also primary elements (earth, water, etc.), cognitive senses and objects, organs of action, and internal organs (mind, ego, etc.). These cosmic components are assigned to the heart, head, tuft, armour, eyes, and weapon (astra) respectively:
1. हृदयाय नमः (heart): ॐ ङक खं गं घं गं नाभौ वाडवग्निवारिभूम्यात्मने हृदयाय नमः॥
2. शिरसे स्वाहा (head): ॐ जं चं छं झं जं शब्दस्पर्शरूपसगन्धात्मने शिरसे स्वाहा ॥
3. शिखायै वषट् (tuft): ॐ णं टं ठं ढं डं श्रोत्रत्वङनेत्रजिह्वाप्रणात्मने शिखायै वषट् ॥
4. कवचाय हूं (armour): ॐ नं तं थं धं दं वाक् पाणिपादपायूपस्थात्मने कवचाय हूं।
5. नेत्रत्रयाय वौषट् (eyes): ॐ मं पं फभंबीं वक्तव्यादानगमनविसर्गनन्दात्मने नेत्रत्रयाय वौषट् ॥
6. अस्त्राय फट् (weapon): ॐ शं यं रं लं हं क्षं सं लं बुद्धिमनोहंकारचित्तात्मने अस्त्राय फट् ॥
sections.summary: This section differentiates between two main types of nyāsa: Rṣyādi-nyāsa, which assigns the core 'limbs' of a mantra (seer, metre, etc.) to the body, and a more complex Ṣaḍaṅga-nyāsa, which maps the entire microcosm of the human body (senses, organs, mind) and the macrocosm (elements) onto the six principal limbs of aṅga-nyāsa.

sections.section_title: Pīṭha-pūjā: Worship of the Deity's Seat
sections.content:
After nyāsa, the next step is `pīṭha-pūjā`, the worship of the deity's seat or pedestal, which is done before the main Nityārcanā. The devotee visualizes a `maṇḍala` (like sarvatobhadra) and imagines the deity in its center, with their guru on the left and Gaṇapati on the right. The worship involves honoring the deities that form the layers of the cosmic pedestal, symbolized by seed-syllables:

1. ॐ मं मण्डूकाय नमः। (Maṇḍūka)
2. ॐ क कालाग्निरुद्राय नमः। (Kālāgnirudra)
3. ॐ अं आधारशक्तये नमः । (Ādhāraśakti)
4. ॐ कूं कूर्माय नमः । (Kūrma - tortoise)
5. ॐ अं अनन्ताय मनः। (Ananta - serpent)
6. ॐ पूं पृथिव्यै नमः । (Pṛthivī - earth)
7. ॐ क्षीं क्षीरसागराय नमः। (Kṣīrasāgara - milky ocean)
8. ॐ रं रत्नद्वीपाय नमः। (Ratnadvīpa - jeweled island)
9. ॐ रं रत्नमण्डपाय नमः । (Ratnamaṇḍapa - jeweled pavilion)
10. ॐ क कल्पवृक्षाय नमः । (Kalpavṛkṣa - wish-fulfilling tree)
11. ॐ रं रत्नवेदिकार्य नमः। (Ratnavedikā - jeweled platform)
12. ॐ रं रत्नसिंहासनाय नमः। (Ratnasiṃhāsana - jeweled throne)

This sequence visualizes a throne built upon layers of cosmic support. The devotee then invokes attendant divinities in the eight directions: Dharma (duty), Jñāna (knowledge), Vairāgya (dispassion), Aiśvarya (lordship), and their opposites Adharma, Ajñāna, Avairāgya, Anaiśvarya.

Finally, the very center of the pedestal is visualized as an abstract lotus representing the entire cosmos. Its components are worshipped as various principles:

1. ॐ आं आनन्दकन्दाय नमः । (Bulb of Bliss)
2. ॐ सं संविन्नालाय नमः । (Stalk of Consciousness)
...and so on for a total of 20 items, including prakṛti (petals), the fifty letters (growths), the solar, lunar, and fire orbs, the three guṇas (sattva, rajas, tamas), different levels of the self (ātman, paramātman, etc.), and ultimate principles (māyā, kāla, vidyā, and paratattva).

The chapter concludes by stating that the deity to be worshipped is, in reality, this formless, supreme principle (`paratattva`), but worship necessitates a concrete representation like an icon or a liṅga.
sections.summary: This final section describes Pīṭha-pūjā, the worship of the deity's divine seat, performed after nyāsa. It involves a complex visualization of the cosmos as a layered throne, starting from foundational deities and building up through cosmic locations to a final abstract lotus. This lotus symbolizes all of existence, from material nature to the ultimate, transcendent principle (paratattva), which is the true object of worship represented by the physical icon.

chapter_summary: Chapter I, "INTRODUCTION," provides a comprehensive overview of the principles and procedures of Hindu daily worship (Nityārcanā) as described in Āgamic and Tāntric texts. It begins by outlining the standard sequences of offerings (upacāras), detailing the sixteen-step (ṣoḍaśopacāra), five-step (pañcopacāra), and three-step variations. The text then elaborates on the specific spiritual and material benefits accrued from each individual offering, drawing from sources like the Śaiva-ratnākara. A significant portion of the chapter is dedicated to the preparatory rites required of the priest, including the mandatory daily prayers (sandhyā), and introduces the crucial concept of Nyāsa—the ritual placement of mantras and divine energies onto the practitioner's body to achieve a state of divinity suitable for worship. Different forms of Nyāsa are explained, including aṅga-nyāsa and kara-nyāsa, and their variations across Vaiṣṇava, Śaiva, and Śrī-vidyā traditions are listed. The chapter culminates in a detailed description of Pīṭha-pūjā, the worship of the deity's cosmic seat, which involves an intricate visualization of the entire universe as a layered throne for the divine. This establishes a foundational principle of the Āgamas: the worship of a physical icon is a means to connect with the formless, supreme, and transcendent reality (paratattva) that underpins all of existence.
key_arguments: Daily worship (Nityārcanā) is a structured, elaborate procedure with defined sequences, each carrying specific benefits.
Proper worship requires the practitioner to undergo purification and preparation, transforming their own body into a divine vessel.
The ritual of Nyāsa is central to this transformation, enabling the devotee to embody divinity before approaching the deity ('nādevo devam arcayet').
The worship space and the deity's seat (pīṭha) are not mere physical objects but are visualized as a microcosm of the entire cosmos.
The ultimate object of worship is the formless, transcendent Supreme Principle (paratattva), for which the physical icon (icon or liṅga) serves as a necessary, concrete focal point.
key_takeaways: Hindu ritual worship is highly systematic, with variations in complexity (16, 5, or 3 steps) to suit different contexts.
Each ritual act is imbued with symbolic meaning and is believed to yield a specific result.
Internal purification and visualization are as important as external actions. Nyāsa is the primary method for this internal divinization.
Ritual practices can vary significantly between different Hindu sects (Vaiṣṇava, Śaiva, Śākta).
The elaborate cosmology of Hindu traditions is mapped onto the ritual process, particularly in the Pīṭha-pūjā, connecting the worshipper to the universe.

quotations.quote: पाद्यार्घ्यचमनीयं च स्नानं वसन वसनभूषणे । ... उपचारास्तुं षोडश ॥
गन्धः सुमं तथा धूपदीपौ नैवेद्यमेव च । पञ्चोपचारा एते स्युर्दीपान्तं वापि सम्मतम्॥
उपवीती बद्धशिखः स्वाचान्तो द्विरनाकुलः । प्राङ्मुख सततं विप्रः सन्ध्योपासनमाचरेत्।।
quotations.context: Stipulating the priest's duties for performing sandhyā.

quotations.quote: सन्ध्या येन न विज्ञाता सन्ध्या येनानुपासिता । जीवमानो भवेच्छूद्रः मृतः श्वा चैव जायते ॥
quotations.context: Emphasizing the importance of performing sandhyā.

quotations.quote: वैदिकीं तु पुरा कृत्वा पश्चाच्छैवमथाचरेत्। दीक्षा संस्कारहीनस्य शुद्धवैदिकमुच्यते ॥
quotations.context: Explaining the sequence of performing Vaidika and Śaiva sandhyā.

quotations.quote: आत्मतत्त्वाय स्वाहा। विद्यातत्त्वाय स्वाहा। शिवतत्त्वाय स्वाहा।
quotations.context: The mantras for ācamana during tāntriki-sandhyā.

quotations.quote: ॐ तत्पुरुषाय विद्महे। महादेवाय धीमहि। तन्नो रुद्रः प्रचोदयात्।।
quotations.context: The Gāyatrī mantra for the tāntriki-sandhyā.
Providing a formal definition of Nyāsa.

quotations.quote: प्रातः काले च वा पूजासमये होमकर्मणि । जपकालेऽपि वा तेषां विनियोगः पृथक् पृथक् ॥
quotations.context: Describing the appropriate times to perform nyāsa.
Explaining the necessity of becoming divine through nyāsa before worshipping a deity.

quotations.quote: आगमोक्तेन विधिना नित्यं न्यासं करोति यः। देवताभावमाप्नोति मन्त्रसिद्धिः प्रजायते ।।
quotations.context: Stating that one who performs nyāsa according to Āgamic rules attains divinity and mantra-siddhi.
